title: More Than 300 Arrested at Palestine Action Protest Outside US Embassy in London
excerpt: The Metropolitan Police said 325 people were arrested at Nine Elms on Saturday, 320 for expressing support for a proscribed organisation, days before a Supreme Court appeal against Palestine Action's ban.
body:
• The Metropolitan Police said 325 people were arrested at Saturday's protest outside the US embassy at Nine Elms in London, 320 of them for expressing support for a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act.
  • Hundreds gathered holding signs reading "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action" in a protest co-ordinated by Defend Our Juries.
  • Defend Our Juries said the arrests took the total detained for defying the ban to more than 4,000 since Palestine Action was proscribed in July 2025; BBC reporting of Home Office figures put the running total at 4,089.
  • The protest came days before a Supreme Court appeal against the ban on November 4; the Home Office says it will robustly defend the proscription, while Amnesty International UK has called for it to be dropped.

More than 300 people were arrested during a protest supporting the banned Palestine Action group outside the US embassy in London, police have said. Hundreds of people gathered at Nine Elms in south-west London on Saturday, many holding signs reading "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action," the BBC reported.

The Metropolitan Police said on Sunday that 325 arrests were made. The force added on social media that 320 of them were for "expressing support for a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act." Expressing support for the group is an offence under the Terrorism Act after it was proscribed in 2025.

How the protest unfolded

Officers began arresting demonstrators one by one around midday on Saturday, sometimes carrying those who refused to walk, and arrests continued into the evening. Protesters were taken to police vans parked on Ponton Road, just off the embassy grounds, to applause and chants of "free, free Palestine" from the crowd, according to the Press Association. Some held signs reading "we are protesters, not terrorists," while one protester climbed a tree outside the embassy waving a placard. A Section 35 dispersal order was in place covering the embassy grounds from 8am to 11pm on Saturday. A parallel demonstration outside the US consulate in Edinburgh drew no arrests, Police Scotland said.

Among those who attended was retired lawyer Charles Allison, 75, who travelled from Cumbria. He told the Press Association he feared for civil liberties, which he said were "being devalued and watered down," and that he hoped the Supreme Court would decide the proscription was unlawful. Defend Our Juries said one of those arrested on Saturday was human rights lawyer Margaret Owen, 94.

The legal fight behind the protest

The protest was organised by Defend Our Juries ahead of an appeal at the Supreme Court against Palestine Action's designation as a terror group on November 4. The group's co-founder was granted permission to appeal the ban, and the court is due to review the proscription under terrorism legislation. On the location, Defend Our Juries said the US had "not shied away" from participation in the Palestine conflict; in August, the US government announced sanctions against Palestine Action, designating it a terror group.

The two sides of the argument were stated plainly over the weekend. The Home Office has said it will robustly defend against the appeal. Defend Our Juries called the arrests "unjust" and an assault on free speech, and its spokesperson described the weekend total as "truly dystopian," arguing the ban was about appeasing the US rather than any terrorist threat. Amnesty International UK criticised the arrests and called for the government to drop the proscription.

Arrests pass 4,000 since the ban

Defend Our Juries, which has been co-ordinating a series of protests over the ban, said Saturday's arrests took the total number of people detained for defying the ban to more than 4,000 since the group was proscribed in July 2025. According to Home Office figures seen by the BBC, 3,630 arrests were made in the year ending June 2026; adding the 134 people arrested outside Westminster Magistrates' Court earlier this year and Saturday's arrests brings the total to 4,089.

What happens next turns on the courts, not the street: the Supreme Court hearing on November 4 will decide whether the challenge to the proscription proceeds, and both the Home Office and the campaigners have set out their positions ahead of it. Further protests are likely either way, given the scale of Saturday's turnout and arrests.
